gap: No result ChatGPT got states that, under USB PD 3.2, the current a charger can supply in the 15–20 V AVS range depends on its rated power. A charger rated 45 W or less either offers AVS only from 9 to 15 V or supplies at most 2.25 A above 15 V. That means a 45 W-class 'AVS' charger cannot supply the roughly 17.4 V at 3 A that the iPhone 18 Pro Max asks for, and the phone falls back to fixed 15 V at about 43 W.
standout_why: I compared the pages ChatGPT cited plus the unsited results. Apple Support (102574) says 'a 60W-capable adapter that uses AVS and supports USB-PD 3.2' but never explains why 60 W is required. Charge-Test gives the request (about 17.4 V at 3 A) and shows that SPR AVS works while EPR AVS gives no benefit, but it does not tie the AVS voltage window or current to the charger's rated power. ChargerLAB's Pro and Pro Max reviews give per-charger readings and the 9–20 V range with no current rule. iThinkDifferent says only 'fine steps'. Both iTechGuides pages say 60 W is needed but give no reason. LTT Labs returned 403. Charge-Test already has part of the finding (the 17.4 V / 3 A request), so the new piece is the rule linking rated power to the AVS window and current.
decides: It confirms that Apple's '60W-capable' wording is an electrical requirement, not marketing. A charger only gives the top tier if it can supply about 3 A at about 17.4 V for a Pro Max, or just under 2.5 A at about 17 V for the smaller Pro, which means it must be rated above 45 W with a 20 V/3 A level. That keeps the Apple 40W Dynamic (60W Max), the UGREEN Nexode Air 65W (measured AVS 9–20 V at 3 A) and the Baseus PicoGo Pro AH22 (AVS 9–20 V at 3 A/5 A) in the top group. It rules out any charger whose port is rated 45 W, even if it says 'AVS'. For our ESR Xtend 45W: ESR says one device can get 5–20 V at up to 3 A, so it may qualify on its own. When both ports are in use it is limited to 45 W total, which by this rule closes the 17 V window. Its own AVS range has not been independently read out, so it should be a qualified row, not a top pick.

findings.label: SPR AVS voltage window and max current by charger rated power (USB PD 3.2)
findings.source_title: USB Type-C Power Delivery Cable Test - GW Instek
findings.note: GW Instek's Table 4 sums up the PD spec. Its exact words: 'The maximum current of the standard power range SPR is determined by 15 volts in the range of 9 to 15 volts; and 20 volts in the range of 15 to 20 volts.' I could not open the USB-IF spec itself (see unsourced).

findings.label: SPR AVS has two separate current fields and fixed voltage steps
findings.value: 9–15 V and 15–20 V current fields; 100 mV voltage step; 50 mA current step in the request
findings.source_title: [PATCH v2 0/3] Add support for AVS in TCPM (Badhri Jagan Sridharan, Google), 2026-03-16
findings.note: The Linux kernel source comment reads 'SPR AVS has two different current ranges 9V - 15V, 15V - 20V'. The constants are SPR_AVS_TIER1_MAX_VOLT_MV=15000, SPR_AVS_TIER2_MAX_VOLT_MV=20000 and SPR_AVS_VOLT_MV_STEP=100. The code takes the 15–20 V maximum from the charger's APDO field pdo_spr_avs_apdo_15v_to_20v_max_current_ma().

findings.label: Arithmetic: why a 45 W 'AVS' charger cannot give the top tier
findings.value: At 17.4 V the phone can draw at most 2.25 A from a 45 W charger: 17.4 V × 2.25 A ≈ 39 W, which is below the 15 V × 3 A = 45 W fixed level. Some 45 W sources advertise AVS only up to 15 V
findings.source_title: Best USB PD 3.2 AVS SPR wall chargers: list and tests - TinkerVault

GW Instek's table gives ≤45 W sources only 9–15 V. Under either reading, a 45 W source cannot supply 3 A at 17.4 V. The arithmetic is mine.
